subject: Re: Stan vs. JAGS, NUTS vs. Gibbs, etc.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: Stan vs. JAGS, NUTS vs. Gibbs, etc.
parts:
1. There are two levels to this evaluation:

a. Gibbs vs. NUTS

b. JAGS vs. Stan

If Gibbs and NUTS have the same complexity, then it
comes down to implementation. If we consider things
like parallelization part of implementation, there
are tradeoffs between Gibbs and NUTS/HMC in that the
former can block parallelize in some cases whereas
NUTS/HMC can parallelize gradient calcs.


2. There are different kinds of scaling issues:

a. number of data items

b. number of parameters

c. number of samples we want

Relative performance will vary. (2c) is especially
important in that NUTS involves a tuning step and
Stan involves a compilation step. Compilation and tuning
both involve up-front costs that are then amortized based
on the number of samples we want.

This is in addition to the scaling in terms of model
complexity, which is itself hard to measure.


3. On that note, there are two things we care about:

a. speed (i.e., wall clock time)

b. space (i.e., memory)

JAGS and Stan have different behaviors here. We'll do real
well scaling on data size in terms of space. If there aren't
involved iterative matrix calcs, we'll also win on parameter
scaling in terms of space.


4. How much tuning do we allow? That is, there are implementation
details within JAGS or Stan that matter. For instance, in
Stan, we can write directly in C++ or use the graphical-model
compiler. If we go with C++, we can use auto-dif or hand-code
our derivatives. If we hand-code derivatives, there are further
optimizations based on whether we use a brute-force adjoint
method or get more clever with intermediate calculations and
sufficient stats. The same holds for JAGS in terms of using
redundant parameters, etc.


- Bob

On 11/21/11 11:33 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> I'm reasonably (but not 100%) confident that if JAGS reverted to
> componentwise slicing then it'd loseï¿½first, because slice sampling
> requires a fair number of log-joint evaluations (I think something like
> 5ï¿½20 per iteration if it's implemented intelligently), and second
> because the slice variables introduce some correlations between time
> steps that analytical Gibbs avoids. But I wouldn't say that's the only
> reason JAGS was winningï¿½this is really a pathologically good model for
> Gibbs due to the very weak correlations. I'm interested to see (do) a
> comparison on a harder problem.
>
> Matt
>
> On Mon, Nov 21, 2011 at 10:59 PM, Andrew Gelman
> <gel...@stat.columbia.edu <mailto:gel...@stat.columbia.edu>> wrote:
>
> One thing I'd like to understand regarding our recent discussions
> is: What is possible in general in problems such as that Bugs
> example where Jags was beating us by a factor of 50? My current
> understanding is that the only reason we're losing is that Jags can
> "cheat" and do exact Gibbs. If, for example, it did componentwise
> slice sampling instead, it wouldn't beat us. Is that correct?
> If so, I think it's ok to lose---or, even better, we should still
> manage to win even there by just being so damn computationally
> efficient. Once we get to really hard problems (our 12-factor model
> for MRP?) maybe we'll have to cheat and do some hard-coded Gibbs
> also, but ideally we can put that off until the last pssible moment.
> A
